subject: Mysuru
text:
Look at the palace in front of you on a Sunday night when ninety-seven thousand electric bulbs turn on at once, drawing the entire building in brilliant light [1, 12]. Why does this city of celebration keep an image of a cursing queen inside its most sacred royal rooms [1]? You might know the feeling of putting on your finest clothes and smiling for a crowd while carrying a private worry you cannot mention to anyone. Mysuru has balanced its public grandeur with a quiet, centuries-old wound since 1610 [1, 8].

Legend has it that a widowed queen named Alamelamma was pursued to the banks of the Kaveri River at Talakad by the new rulers of Mysuru who wanted her temple jewels [1]. Before she plunged into the cold, rushing water, she spoke a three-part curse: let the town of Talakad turn to sand, let the nearby river turn to whirlpools, and let the kings of Mysuru never bear children [1].

Set the legend aside and look at the record. Geologists say the sand that buried Talakad was just the river shifting course and wind moving dune fields [1]. Yet, the Wadiyar succession has repeatedly gone sideways; Chamaraja Wadiyar the Tenth came to the throne by adoption in the nineteenth century, and the line passed by adoption again as recently as 2015 [1]. The royal family took this so seriously that they installed her image inside the palace to honour her [1]. As the electric lights flicker out, look up at the dark outline of Chamundi Hill watching over the quiet city [2].

Why would a proud city name itself after the monster that terrorised it, rather than the goddess who saved them [5, 18]? The story goes that a buffalo demon named Mahishasura ruled this land until the goddess Chamundeshwari came down to the hill above the plains and killed him [5, 18]. Yet, if you walk the road up that hill today, you will find a bright, painted statue of the demon standing with a sword in one hand, a cobra in the other, and an immaculate moustache [3]. Locals treat this ancient enemy with a strange, protective fondness [3]. We all carry our own quiet scars while trying to show the world a brave, beautiful face, balancing our private wounds against our public celebrations [4].

Some historians argue the name Mysuru has nothing to do with a demon's defeat, claiming it simply comes from an old term for buffalo country [5]. Yet the city rejects this dry explanation, choosing to keep the monster's name and celebrate his end every autumn [5]. This tension between cold facts and living stories shapes the very streets you walk on [6].

To see how deeply this contradiction is carved into the earth, stand at the front of the palace and look east toward the green slopes of Chamundi Hill [24, 9]. The palace faces the hill directly because the Wadiyar kings wanted their home to look straight at the temple of their protector [2]. On a clear morning, you can smell the faint scent of wild grass on the wind and easily pick out the temple tower rising over the plains [24, 9]. The kings built this grand stage with wide, straight roads to hold their festival of victory, keeping their eyes fixed on the heights where the battle was won [24, 9].

Can you celebrate a grand future while carrying a wound you cannot heal? In 1897, the regent queen Kempananjammanni watched her family's wooden palace burn to ash during a royal wedding [7]. She refused to rebuild with vulnerable wood, hiring architect Henry Irwin to raise a fortress of stone, iron, and glass [7]. If you stand in the wedding hall today, you can look up at a ceiling of turquoise and green stained glass made in Glasgow, held up by massive Scottish iron pillars [8]. Touch one of these pillars; it is cold iron painted to look like carved stone [8]. We all build beautiful things to show the world we are fine, even while guarding against a fire we dread.

But some fires cannot be stopped by iron, and people here say the royal family carries a much darker scar. The story goes that in 1610, a widowed queen named Alamelamma was pursued by the new rulers of Mysuru to the banks of the Kaveri River [1]. Before she threw herself into the water, she cursed the dynasty: let their lands turn to sand, and let the kings of Mysuru never bear children [1]. Today, the town of Talakad is indeed buried under dunes of sand, and for generations, the royal family has had to adopt its heirs [1]. Inside the palace, the family still honours an image of the queen who cursed them [1]. They do not take chances.

This is the secret trick of Mysuru: it holds its grandest celebrations and its deepest wounds in the very same hand [4]. On Sunday nights, close to a lakh of electric bulbs suddenly switch on, drawing the entire palace in brilliant, blinding light [4]. The city ran on electricity before most of Europe, drawing power from the Kaveri River—the same water that claimed the cursed queen [9][1]. You are standing in a place where the lights are for everyone, but the curse is family business [4]. As the bulbs flicker out, they leave only the dark outline of Chamundi Hill watching over a family still waiting for an heir [4][2].

A life-sized mechanical tiger grunts as it mauls a carved British soldier in a quiet London museum gallery [10]. This savage toy was the pride of Tipu Sultan, the ruler who fought the British with iron-cased rockets from his river-walled island capital of Srirangapatna until he died in the breach in 1799 [3, 7, 10]. Today, the British still keep his tiger as a trophy, a permanent display of Mysuru’s historical wounds [10]. You might know what it is like to put your finest achievements on display while quietly hiding the scars of an old defeat. Here, the grand palace in front of you was built of stone and iron for a queen who had just watched her wooden home burn to the ground [7].

The story goes that this royal grandeur carries a dark price that the family still takes seriously [1, 17]. In 1610, a widowed queen named Alamelamma fled to the Kaveri River to protect her temple jewels from the new rulers of Mysuru [1]. Before she drowned herself in the swirling water, she cursed the dynasty: let their lands turn to sand, and let the kings of Mysuru never bear children [1]. Geologists note that wind and river shifts naturally buried the nearby town of Talakad in sand dunes, but the royal family did not take chances [6, 17]. For four hundred years, generation after generation, the Wadiyar kings have had to adopt their heirs to keep the throne [6, 17].

To survive their losses, the family turned to trade and public spectacle [8, 12]. When a world war halted sandalwood exports in 1916, the king built a factory to turn the wood into soap, filling the air with the rich, creamy scent you can still smell in the markets today [11]. In the palace kitchens, a cook named Madappa mixed gram flour, ghee, and sugar syrup to create Mysore pak, a sweet that melts on your tongue [12]. On Sunday nights, close to a lakh of electric bulbs suddenly snap on, drawing the entire palace in brilliant lines of fire against the dark sky [4]. Look up at the glowing walls before the lights flicker out, leaving only the silent outline of Chamundi Hill watching over the quiet city [1, 24].
